name: Zane Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a senior buyer at Meridian Auto Parts, a distributor of brake pads, filters, batteries and body panels that sells to garages and repair chains. I open the day with an AI assistant that summarises overnight price changes and flags parts running low across our four warehouses. Then I make calls to manufacturers, mostly to push on price and delivery dates, and I spend a chunk of the afternoon on forecasts. I'm curious about tools, so I'm often the one trying something new on the team.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out, and what do you like most?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The tiring part is the shift to electric cars, because every year a few combustion parts sell less, and I have to guess how fast. I like the numbers game, and I like that garages actually depend on us, since a car sitting on a ramp costs them money. My partner Elise is a product designer at a furniture company, and we're renting a flat and spending weekends restoring an old motorbike.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good tool that has some limits, and that the people predicting a revolution have mostly sold something. At work I'd carry on sharing tips and say it's worth using for the dull jobs. Online I'd comment sometimes, mostly to correct exaggeration.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be pretty calm. My skills with the tools would keep me ahead, and the job is still about judgment and relationships. My own worry is the electric car transition, which cuts demand for some of our biggest product lines, and that doesn't depend on AI at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the assistant and keep trying new tools in small ways. I'd save a third of my pay and add to an index fund. Elise and I would probably look at buying a flat in the next two years, and I'd finish the restoration of that motorbike.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a small itch about the electric car shift. It's a world I understand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the electric car shift mean for your purchasing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fewer exhaust parts, fewer oil filters, more batteries and sensors, and customers who don't know yet what to stock. I'd spend a lot of time guessing the pace, and if I guess wrong we hold dead stock. It's a bigger worry for me than any chatbot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the new tool you'd try next?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something that predicts garage demand from local car registrations and weather. It's nothing magic, but I think it could shave a few percent off our stock. If it works, I'd show the team and see if the boss will pay for it.

say: I'd say AI is a **good tool with limits**, and the revolution talk is mostly selling.
At work I'd share tips and say it's worth using for **dull jobs**.
think: I'd be **pretty calm**, since my skills with the tools keep me ahead.
My real worry is the **electric car transition**, which cuts demand for big product lines.
do: I'd keep using the **assistant** and trying new tools in small ways.
I'd save **a third** of my pay and add to an index fund.
I'd look at buying a **flat** with Elise within two years.
feel: I feel **calm** with a small itch about the electric car shift.

fieldNote: His one real concern is the **electric car transition**, which is independent of AI.
He is a **tool tester** who looks for a few percent in savings.
He stays calm because his skills put him **ahead** of colleagues.

Save a third of pay each month
Add to the index fund and aim for a flat deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the routine buying is going to software and the sensible move is to decide who manages it. I'd tell friends that it's real change, with winners and losers. Online I'd say retraining should be tax-deductible and easy to access.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel uneasy. I'm better placed than most because I use the tools daily, but our team of six would likely shrink, and the juniors who check orders would go first. The company would also want to know why a buyer costs what a buyer costs, when software can do the reorders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer to build the rules for an automated ordering system, so I'm the person who knows what's inside it. I'd pick up a course in data analysis, to be able to check what the software does. I'd also keep spending flat and boost savings, and talk to a recruiter I know about what firms are hiring for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but motivated. It's the kind of change I'd rather be inside of than watching from the side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said juniors who check orders would go first. Who do you have in mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two people, Dara and Pieter, who've been with us about a year. They do the clean-up work that software handles best, and they're good, but quick tools make good and cheap look similar. I'd try to get them onto exception handling, which is harder to automate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why talk to a recruiter now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's smart to know your market before you need it. Recruiters see which roles are shrinking before the rest of us do, and the call costs me nothing. I'd do the same in any version of this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening far faster than anything built to handle it, and that we need emergency decisions on income support and notice periods. At work I'd say we should assume jobs are changing now. Online I'd back anyone with a practical plan, whichever party they're from.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd expect most of my current role to be done by software within two years, since it's all thinking and numbers. My strengths are speed with tools and the ability to switch fields, but a general AI beats me at both. The robots come three years later, and the electric car shift adds to the squeeze on parts sales.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move quickly. I'd set aside a year of costs, cut subscriptions and big purchases, and look for work close to physical things: running a warehouse, or a customer-facing role at a garage chain. I'd ask Elise about whether her company would let her go part-time to learn something new, because two incomes at risk is a lot. I'd also try to sell my skills as an AI consultant to small garages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and a bit buzzed. It's the biggest change of my life and I can't pretend I'd stay calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned consulting for small garages. What would you offer them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Simple things: automating their parts ordering, spotting dead stock, and cutting the time they spend on the phone. They're small, busy and not tech people. I'd charge a modest monthly fee and see if it covers even part of my costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you say two incomes at risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Elise is a designer, and design is exactly the sort of work the card means. We both sit on the desk side of the economy. A hands-on job on the side, or a hands-on partner, would be a good hedge, but we'd have neither.

fieldNote: The household has **two desk incomes**, which is the heart of his anxiety.

His honesty about being **beaten** by a general AI at his own strengths stands out.

Apply for warehouse or garage-chain operations roles

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to prepare if we act now, so I'd push for retraining funds and clear rules. At work I'd propose a written roadmap. I'd tell friends to build a skill that involves hands or people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel steadier than in the two-year case. I'd be thirty-two and I could cross into a new field in that time. But I'd also know many will do the same, and the jobs that survive will be competitive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first year running my consulting side project to see if it works. In parallel I'd start a part-time course in logistics operations, to get closer to hands-on work. I'd buy a flat in a mid-priced area, because owning gives stability if pay falls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but optimistic. Five years feels like a real chance to land well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why logistics and not something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it combines thinking with physical flow: trucks, warehouses, people. The thinking parts will be automated, but the physical parts take longer, and the people who understand both will be valuable for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as proof that the side project works?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five paying garages by month twelve, and a profit after tool costs. If I hit that, it's real. If not, I stop, and I haven't lost much but weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is plenty of time to adapt. I'd say at work that we should run it as a long-term plan, review yearly, and keep skills fresh. Online I'd say everyone should be trying the tools now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be calm. I'd be thirty-seven with a decade of practice in using these tools and plenty of time to build a second career or a small business. I'd still keep an eye on how quickly things move, but I wouldn't feel hunted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and keep learning, buy the flat, and put a decent sum into index funds. I'd grow my side business, probably into a small software service for garages. Elise and I would plan to start a family in a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and positive. It's a long run-up and I'd treat it as a chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the software service do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would help garages see what parts they use most and order them at the right time, so they don't tie up money in a shelf of rarely used parts. If it worked, I could imagine ten or twenty customers and a bit of extra income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave your job for it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not unless it replaced my salary. I'd rather keep the job while it's solid and use it to fund the side project. But with ten years of warning, I'd feel free to try.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because it's too quick for the systems around us, like schools, tax and health cover, to keep up. What would help is practical: retraining that's paid for and linked to real jobs, and maybe a more flexible safety net for people between jobs. I'd also like companies to say plainly what they plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how much of this I'm already living. I use these tools every day and I've seen colleagues who don't. The gap is widening, and nobody wants to talk about it at work.
